reconcile.connective: The commentators read Isaiah's outburst as aimed at hypocritical, sin-laden worship, not at the Sabbath institution the law makes perpetual.

discrepancy.connective: Julius Wellhausen presses the harder reading: he takes Isaiah's words (with Amos and Jeremiah) as evidence that the prophets did not regard the elaborate festal cult — sacrifices, new moons, sabbath assemblies — as something Yahweh had ever commanded, against the Priestly law that makes it a standing obligation.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Because they had not performed what Jehovah commanded as He commanded it, He expressly forbids them to continue it.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the tension: the prohibition in Isa 1:13 is not a repeal of the commanded Sabbath/festal observance but a rejection of it because it was performed wrongly.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The Lord wanted Judah to stop the religious exercises he had commanded them to do rather than to continue them in a manner that was sinful and false (1:13).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the harmonization plainly: the same God commanded the exercises and now rejects them, the difference being the sinful, false manner of observance, not the obligation.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Although God commanded these sacrifices for a time, as aids and exercises of their faith: yet because the people had not faith nor repentance, God detesteth them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames the apparent conflict as God-commanded worship rejected for the worshippers' lack of faith and repentance, not abrogation of the command itself.

pd_work.note: K&D treat this passage directly, arguing the prohibition targets festivals 'associated with wickedness' — 'Because they had not performed what Jehovah commanded as He commanded it, He expressly forbids them to continue it' — not the standing Sabbath/festal obligation.
